title: Social and Economic Contributors to Neonatal Outcome in the United States

paragraphs.text: 8 Social and Economic Contributors to Neonatal Outcome in the United States
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Although there have been significant improvements in infant mortality (death within 1 year of life) and neonatal mortality (death within 28 days of life) in the United States over the past 50 years, compared with other highincome countries in the world, the United States alarmingly lags behind these other countries in infant mortality rates.1 Infant mortality and morbidity rates are commonly used as an important indicator worldwide of overall population health. Recent research has focused on why the United States has not seen continued improvements in these public health indices as have other countries, and indeed several markers of US infant health have worsened in recent years. It is important to understand recent US trends and contributing factors to provide optimal care and public health planning in the prenatal, perinatal, neonatal, and postneonatal periods to improve these outcomes. One major factor contributing to these poor perinatal and infant outcomes in the United States is the significant health disparities seen among women and infants related to race and ethnicity. Other disparities in health outcomes in the perinatal and infant period in the United States are related to poverty, poor maternal health, lack of health care access and health insurance, and other overall indicators of poor socioeconomic status.
paragraphs.heading: Epidemiology of Health Disparities in Neonatal and Perinatal Medicine

paragraphs.text: Although the United States had a steady decline in infant mortality over the past decades, declining 19% from 6.89 deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 5.58 per 1000 in 2019
paragraphs.heading: Infant Mortality

paragraphs.text: (Fig. 8.1),2 this rate is still almost twice that of other comparable countries in the world. Recent data comparing infant mortality indicated that the United States had two to three times the infant mortality rate of countries such as Japan, Italy, and Sweden1 in spite of significantly larger health care expenditures in the United States per capita compared with these other countries.3 Multiple studies have attempted to delineate the factors unique to the United States that might explain this discrepancy. The United States has made continued progress in decreasing the neonatal mortality rate as well, with a rate of 3.69 per 1000 births in 2019, a significant decrease from 4.62 per 1000 births documented in 2000.2 However, this rate is also significantly higher than the neonatal mortality rates seen in comparable countries.
paragraphs.heading: Infant Mortality

paragraphs.text: Prematurity (infants born at less than 37 weeks) overall in the United States has a major impact on the high infant mortality rates. Previous studies show that the United States has rates of prematurity two to three times that of other developed countries.4 Clearly this is a significant contributor to the high infant mortality seen in the United States. During the 1990s and early 2000s, the US preterm birth rate steadily increased by 20% from 10.6% in 1990 to 12.8% in 2006.5 At that time, after widespread public health efforts, it seemed the United States was making significant progress in decreasing the rate of prematurity. paragraphs.text: Given that the percentage overall of preterm births in the United States is twice that of comparable countries, addressing the causes of prematurity are critical to reducing the US infant mortality rate. However, a higher rate of prematurity alone does not explain the higher US infant mortality rate because the gestational age specific infant mortality rates are also increased above other countries at gestational ages 32 weeks and greater, the category with the highest number of preterm births as well as term births.4,6 Addressing prematurity is a significant financial priority as well as public health priority. Recent estimates from a large commercially insured population (763,566 infants) reveal that the cost for the median term birth for the first 6 months of life was $3787, whereas for a premature infant born at 24 weeks, the median cost for the first 6 months is $548,865.8 It was estimated that in recent years, more than $25 billion is spent each year on premature births.9

paragraphs.text: It is now well established that a major contributor to the concerning infant mortality rates in the United States is the significant health disparities seen in the country. The major health disparity is related to racial and ethnic differences seen in numerous aspects of infant and perinatal health outcomes in all states in the United States, with wide variation state to state. Epidemiologists have carefully tracked infant mortality rates by race and ethnicity in the United States for many years and have documented significant differences in neonatal and infant mortality by race and ethnicity, worsening in recent years. Indeed, over the past 100 years in the United States, while the neonatal and post-neonatal mortality rates for both non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic

paragraphs.text: Black have improved, the Black/White ratios of mortality have steadily worsened and remained high over the past 100 years.1 Studies have generally gathered data according to the following racial and ethnic distinctions with a variation in naming in multiple references: non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Asian or Pacific Islander. More recent data have separated Pacific Islanders from the Asian outcomes, with the realization that these are actually very different groups with different outcomes.2,6 In addition, Hispanic groups are often further subcategorized by Hispanic origin: Puerto Rican, Mexican, Central and South American, and Cuban.2 Several studies have also investigated if race and ethnicity are impacted by whether the mother is US or foreign born.10 These studies have shown a worse outcome for the same racial groups if born in the United States compared with being foreign born, both for Hispanics and non- Hispanic Blacks.

paragraphs.text: Recent epidemiologic studies have consistently shown that non-Hispanic Black infants have an infant mortality rate greater than two times that of non-Hispanic White infants (10.62 deaths per 1000 live births in 2019 vs. 4.49 per 1000 live births) (Fig. 8.3).2 American Indian or Alaskan Native and Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander infants also exhibit substantially higher infant mortality rates than non-Hispanic Whites.2 Past infant mortality data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) grouped Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander infants with Asian infants and indicated low infant mortality rates,11 but recent studies separating these groups from Asian infants indicate that Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander outcomes for infant mortality are much more similar to American Indian

paragraphs.text: or Alaska Native outcomes.2 Interestingly, Asian infants have consistently exhibited the lowest neonatal and infant mortality rates for many years, whereas Hispanic infant mortality rates track close to non-Hispanic White infant mortality rates, in spite of economic disadvantages and poor health care access for many Hispanic women and infants.2
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 8.2 Preterm birth rates: United States, final 2007 to 2019 and provisional 2020. (From National

paragraphs.text: As noted, overall infant mortality rates in total and for each race or ethnic group have decreased each year.2,11 It appeared that the United States was making great strides in reducing the discrepancies in infant mortality rates related to race with a 20% decline from 2005 to 2014 seen in non-Hispanic Black rates compared to the overall US decline of 16% during those years. However, recent US infant mortality data show disturbingly that in 2019, only non-Hispanic Whites had a significant decrease; other groups did not show a statistically significant improvement.2 Of concern, the 2019 data indicate that for non-Hispanic Black infants compared to non-Hispanic White infants, the infant mortality rate disparity increased from 2.24 in 2014 to 2.37 in 2019. The disparity in neonatal mortality for non-Hispanic Black infants compared to non-Hispanic White infants also is disturbingly high at 2.35. However, a different picture emerges for neonatal and infant mortality rates of Native American/Alaska Natives and Native Hawaiian/ Pacific Islanders. These two groups have also had higher infant mortality rates compared to non-Hispanic White infants (see Fig. 8.3). However, for both non-Hispanic White and Black infants the contribution to infant mortality of deaths for the postneonatal period is similar at about 35%, while for Pacific Islanders it is increased to almost 40% of infant mortality and for American Indian or Alaska Native infants, the contribution to infant mortality in the postneonatal period is almost 50%.2 Thus it is likely that there are differences in each of these racial groups for the higher infant mortality rates compared to non-Hispanic White infants and it appears that in the United States, these disparities by race are worsening in recent years. As noted, infant mortality rates for Hispanics track closely with those of non-Hispanic White infants. Interestingly, when looking closely at the infant and neonatal mortality rates in Hispanics by ethnicity, wide ranges exist, with Cuban Hispanic infants having a much lower infant mortality rate compared to Puerto Rican Hispanic infants in 2019 (4.14 per 1,000 live births compared to 6.17 per 1,000 live births.2 In addition, there are significant differences in infant mortality by state in the United States, with the southern states having the highest infant mortality. These are also the states with the highest percentage of non-Hispanic Black women in their population (Fig. 8.4). In addition, those states with the greatest increase in level of income inequality in recent years have higher risks of infant and neonatal mortality.12

paragraphs.text: It is also important to evaluate perinatal mortality rates (late fetal deaths at 28 completed weeks of gestation or more and early neonatal deaths less than age 7 days) because this can be an indicator of the quality of health care before, during, and after delivery and also of the health status of the nation. In addition, late fetal deaths are not accounted for in neonatal and infant mortality and may skew infant mortality rates when evaluating by race. Similar to infant mortality in
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 8.2 Preterm birth rates: United States, final 2007 to 2019 and provisional 2020. (From National

paragraphs.text: the United States, there was a significant decrease in perinatal mortality in the United States from 1990 to 2011, which did not improve over the next 5 years. Encouragingly, there has been a small but significant decrease in perinatal mortality since 2017 in both late fetal and early neonatal deaths.13 However, mirroring the infant mortality rate disparities, fetal deaths and perinatal mortality rates show wide ranges when looking closely at race and ethnicity. Non-Hispanic Black fetal mortality rates are twice as high as non-Hispanic White rates.13 Poorer maternal health and decreased access to prenatal care may have an impact on this outcome.

paragraphs.text: To understand the impact of race and ethnicity on neonatal and infant mortality in the United States, we must first understand whether differences exist in maternal and prenatal factors that would impact mortality. Similar to the significant racial disparities seen in infant mortality, the incidence of prematurity (babies less than 37 weeks) varies greatly by race and ethnicity. Non-Hispanic Black women consistently have the highest rate of overall prematurity, and it was almost 60% higher than the prematurity rates of non-Hispanic White women in 2020.6 The disparities in the incidence of severe prematurity also increase greatly by race and ethnicity, with the percentage of births less than 28 weeks (the risk of highest mortality) in 2020 for non-Hispanic Blacks being more than three times the percent of non-Hispanic Whites in 2020 (1.47% vs. 0.44%).6 When evaluating the impact of prematurity on mortality, those born at the lowest gestational ages have the highest mortality. Similar to infant mortality outcomes, the highest prematurity rate of infants born less than 34 weeks occurs for non-Hispanic Black infants (4.82 %) compared with non-Hispanic Whites (2.21%). The lowest prematurity rate of infants less than 34 weeks is seen in Asian infants (2.08%), with Hispanic infants (2.52%) slightly greater than those of non-Hispanic Whites (Table 8.1). American Indian/Alaskan Native infants and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander infants show a more favorable less than 34-week percentage at 3.05% and 3.08% of births, respectively, in 2020 compared with the rate for non-Hispanic Black infants.6 As noted previously, overall US prematurity rates for less than 37 weeks’ gestation are increased in recent years compared with the lowest rate in 2014, and we will need to carefully investigate the contribution of racial disparities to this recent increase in prematurity.6,7 Similar to the wide variation in infant mortality by state in the United States, there are vast differences state by state in the rate of prematurity in the United States, with Southern states having the highest preterm rates (see Fig. 8.4).

paragraphs.text: Whites at almost four times the rate. Compared with non-Hispanic White infants, non-Hispanic Black infants also die at a disproportionate rate because of congenital malformations and newborns affected by maternal complications of pregnancy. In contrast, Native Americans and Alaska Natives have a much lower infant mortality because of prematurity compared with other groups but have the highest rate of infant deaths because of SIDS of all racial and ethnic groups examined. There are also differences in mortality noted within certain ethnic groups. For Puerto Rican infants, the rate of infant mortality because of preterm causes is almost twofold that of non-Hispanic Whites and is the highest among the Hispanic subgroups, with Central (Mexico) and South Americans having much lower rates of prematurity and infant mortality.2 This could reflect the longerterm presence of the Puerto Rican population in the United States compared with more recent Hispanic immigrants and the cumulative toxic effect in the United States of low socioeconomic status over time on adverse pregnancy outcomes.

paragraphs.text: Congenital anomalies and subsequent infant mortality are also impacted by health disparities. Bassil et al. found that

paragraphs.text: socioeconomic inequities lead to a significant increase in major congenital anomalies in babies born to mothers in areas of highest deprivation.14 Further analysis revealed that there were higher odds of chromosomal and multiple systems anomalies in the highest deprivation areas. These findings could be explained by higher exposure to teratogens or to poor health of these disadvantaged mothers. A more recent study from California found that increased social deprivation and exposures to environmental pollutants are associated with a higher incidence of congenital heart disease.15 Minorities in the United States are often the racial groups living in the poorest neighborhoods, with increased exposure to pollution and environmental toxins.

paragraphs.text: Postneonatal mortality in SIDS and SUID, leading and increasing causes of infant mortality, also exhibit racial and ethnic disparities. Sharp declines in the rates of SIDS in the 1990s have been associated with national efforts to promote infant safe sleep, mainly through the Back-to-Sleep campaign.16 In addition, cases previously diagnosed as SIDS deaths are now being classified as unknown or accidental strangulation in bed. Therefore the encompassing term of SUID captures the true
paragraphs.heading: Selected Maternal and Birth Characteristics by Race and Hispanic Origin of Mother, 2020 Final Data. National Center for Health Statistics

paragraphs.text: trend of these deaths more accurately. However, racial disparities in SIDS/SUID have persisted. For American Indian or Alaska Natives, the largest difference in infant mortality outcomes when compared with non-Hispanic Whites is the almost threefold increase in mortality rate in 2020 caused by SIDS from recent data (American Indian: 84.4 per 100,000 live births, non-Hispanic White: 28.9 per 100,000 live births)2 compared with a slight increase in mortality rate because of prematurity for American Indian or Alaska Natives when compared with White infants.2 Similar to overall infant mortality, non-Hispanic Black infants also have a very high rate of death caused by SIDS seen in 2020, only slightly less than that of American Indian or Alaska Natives. Similar racial disparities for American Indian or Alaska Natives are seen in SUID. For American Indian or Alaska Natives, the largest difference in mortality outcomes when compared with non- Hispanic Whites is the twofold increase in deaths caused by SUID (American Indian: 177.6 per 100,000 live births, non-Hispanic White: 84.5 per 100,000 live births).17 Non- Hispanic Blacks also have an extremely high rate of mortality from SUID (172.4 per 100,000 live births), only slightly lower than the rate for Native American infants.17 The lowest rate of SUID is seen in Hispanic and Asian/Pacific Islander infants (Hispanic: 49.3 per 100,000 live births, Asian/Pacific Islanders: 28.3 per 100,000 live births), even lower than the non-Hispanic White rate. A significant impact on SUID is decreasing gestational age at birth, with infants born at 24 to 27 weeks having a 3.5- to 5-fold increase in the rate of SIDS compared with term infants.18 Again, racial disparities are seen here, with a SUID rate in non-Hispanic Blacks at less than 28 weeks of 382.3 per 100,000 live births compared with the lowest group Asian/Pacific Islanders: 126.6 per 100,000 live births at less than 28 weeks.17 Given that the highest rate of prematurity is seen in non-Hispanic Blacks, this contribution to SIDS/SUID also negatively impacts this population and infant mortality. It is unclear what impact genetic versus cultural factors may play in mortality caused by SUID and SIDS. Finally, there has been a distressing increase in infant mortality because of accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed (ASSB) over more than 20 years.19 A recent study has shown that ASSB mortality continues to increase significantly: for 1999 to 2016, 4.4-fold for non-Hispanic Black girls (45.8 per 100,000 in 2016), 3.5-fold for non-Hispanic Black boys (53.8), 2.7-fold for non-Hispanic White girls (15.8), and 4.0-fold for non-Hispanic White boys (25.9). As for many other factors impacting the racial inequities impacting infant mortality, the overall rates were much higher for non-Hispanic Black infants. The authors also noted factors previously associated with ASSB (unmarried mothers and mothers with low educational attainment, low infant birth weight, low gestational age, lack of prenatal care) continue to be associated with both overall ASSB and racial inequalities adversely affecting non-Hispanic Black infants.

paragraphs.text: Maternal mortality related to pregnancy has been steadily increasing in the United States over the past 20 years and
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: continues to increase20,21 despite significant decreases seen in other high-income countries during this same time period.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: A maternal death is defined by the World Health Organization as “the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and the site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.” Again, alarming racial and ethnic disparities are seen in pregnancy-related mortality in the United States, with non-Hispanic Black women dying at a rate almost three times that of non-Hispanic White women (55.3/100,000 live births vs. 19.1/100,000).20 This is especially concerning for pregnant non-Hispanic Black women over the age of 40, with a rate of 263.1 per 100,000 live births.20 The higher maternal mortality rates for Black women are consistent regardless of education level.22 For Native American and Alaska Natives mothers, similar to the high infant mortality rates, the maternal mortality rates are more than twice that of non-Hispanic White mothers.22 Maternal mortality rates have also increased over the past years for Hispanic mothers, but their rates are similar to, and even slightly lower than, non-Hispanic White mothers.22 Although the reasons for the dramatic increase in US pregnancy related mortality and morbidity are not clearly understood, underlying poorer maternal health, obesity, lack of prenatal care, poor access to medical care, inadequate or no health insurance, teen pregnancies, and single mothers without support systems all are likely contributors to this high mortality rate. Maternal morbidities and other indicators of poor health care during pregnancy are significantly higher in non-Hispanic Black women and American Indian and Alaskan Native women compared with Non-Hispanic White women.6,23,24 Maternal deaths caused by hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, emboli, and anesthesia complications have declined because of state initiatives and focused educational and obstetric interventions; however, contributions to maternal death from cardiovascular conditions, cardiomyopathy, stroke, and noncardiovascular medical conditions have significantly increased in recent years.24 Looking more closely at severe maternal morbidity during the delivery period and post delivery in the Medicaid population, non- Hispanic Black women (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.53), Hispanic women (aOR, 1.46), and women of other races or ethnicities (aOR, 1.40) had higher rates of morbidity during delivery hospitalization than non-Hispanic White women; however, only the disparity between Black and White women (aOR, 1.69; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.57–1.81) persisted into the postdischarge period.23 Racial disparities impact a variety of maternal morbidities, with non-Hispanic Black and American Indian and Alaska Native women having the highest rates of blood transfusion, heart failure, shock, eclampsia, and renal failure in the perinatal period, as well as an overall rate of severe maternal morbidity more than twice that of non- Hispanic White women during delivery hospitalization.24 Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are particularly dangerous conditions leading to maternal morbidity and death, as well as several neonatal complications, especially preterm birth and its associated complications for the neonate. The rates of
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: hypertensive disorders of pregnancy as well as chronic hypertension in women during their pregnancies have dramatically increased in the past 30 years.25 Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are highest in non-Hispanic Black mothers and American Indians/Alaska Natives but lower in Hispanics and Asians compared with non-Hispanic White women.26 However, in a study looking at more than 11 million deliveries in the United States from 2016 to 2018, although Black women were the most likely to experience preeclampsia, Asian/Pacific women were the most at risk for acute cardiovascular complications during delivery hospitalization.26 In addition, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and subsequent elective deliveries because of maternal risks are a leading cause of prematurity.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: As noted, the worsening health of many women before and during pregnancy has been a leading cause of poor maternal and infant outcomes.25 The massive rise in obesity in the US population over the past years has been well documented. Of significant concern to those in the public health arena is how this has negatively impacted women of productive age and their future children. Maternal obesity is another aspect of health disparities in that those races and ethnicities exhibiting worse perinatal and neonatal outcomes also have significantly higher rates of obesity than the general population. Recent data indicate that in the past decade, non-Hispanic Black women older than the ages of 20 have an extremely high incidence of obesity at 56.9% compared with non-Hispanic White women at 39.8%.27 Hispanic women also suffer from this epidemic of increased weight with a recent obesity incidence of 43.7%. In recent years, the rate of prepregnancy obesity has increased significantly in spite of the known health risks during pregnancy. Disparities in the incidence of obesity during pregnancy also are seen in non-Hispanic Black women who have the highest rates of obesity before and during pregnancy in the general population, especially at the highest categories of obesity. From 2016 to 2019, the percentage of non-Hispanic White women with prepregnancy obesity rose 10% (from 24.1% to 26.6%), 7% for non-Hispanic Black women (36.4%–39.1%), and 12% for Hispanic women (28.9%–32.4%).28 Obesity is known to increase the risk of gestational diabetes from a baseline of 2.8% to a high of 14.6% in pregnant women with class III obesity.29 Other morbidities of pregnancy such as gestational hypertensive disorders (increasing fourfold at highest obesity classes), infection, cesarean section rates, and cardiovascular events are all higher in obese pregnant women. Although obesity has its own risks of increased morbidity in pregnant women, obesity is also associated with increased neonatal/infant mortality and morbidity, as well as preterm delivery and congenital malformations.28 Infant mortality increases with each increase in obesity category. Declercq et al. found that with a normal prepregnancy weight as a reference, the odds ratio (OR) for an infant death rose from 1.32 for mothers in the obese I category up to 1.73 for obese III category pregnant mothers.30 Lemon et al. reported that compared with non-Hispanic White women, non-Hispanic Black women were more likely to have obesity and experienced a higher rate of stillbirth (8.3 vs. 3.6 stillbirths per 1000 liveborn and stillborn infants) and infant death (8.5 vs. 3.0 infant deaths per 1000 live births).31
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: In addition, obesity during pregnancy also is associated with increased neonatal morbidities such as increased prematurity, sepsis, large for gestational age infants, and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission.29 Increasing obesity also results in an increased risk of major malformations in the neonate and were the highest as the severity of obesity increased.32 Congenital malformations were seen in the cardiovascular system, malformations of the nervous system, and limb defects. Clearly, the obesity epidemic is adversely affecting minority women during pregnancy and their babies disproportionately. It is also likely that an impact to reduce these adverse outcomes must be implemented before conception to impact these events which develop even before most mothers realize they are pregnant.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: Separate from its relation to obesity, there has also been a significant increase in diabetes during pregnancy, both for type I and II diabetes before pregnancy and gestational diabetes during pregnancy.25,33 Diabetes during pregnancy leads to significant poor outcomes for the mother, as well as for the fetus and infant. Severe maternal diabetes at the time of conception can result in major congenital anomalies. Diabetes during the pregnancy can result in cardiac anomalies, birth asphyxia, and severe hypoglycemia in the neonate. However, there are known racial and ethnic differences in gestational diabetes. A recent study of gestational diabetes by Shah et al. found that, among individuals with a singleton first live birth in the United States from 2011 to 2019, rates of gestational diabetes increased across all racial and ethnic subgroups, overall by 3.7% per year. Gestational diabetes rates were highest in Asian Indian mothers, and among Hispanic/Latina participants, gestational diabetes rates were highest among Puerto Rican individuals.33 However, this study did not include American Indians/Alaska Natives, a group known to have extremely high rates of both pre-existing diabetes and gestational diabetes.34 In addition, this study also found that non- Hispanic Black mothers had the highest rate of pregestational diabetes, more than 50% higher than non-Hispanic White mothers (14.2 per 1000 live births compared with 7.9).33
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: A significant body of research has focused on the high teen pregnancy rate in the United States compared with other high-income countries. In the United States, babies born to mothers younger than the age of 20 have the highest infant mortality rates,2,35 with those mothers at the lowest ages having even higher infant mortality rates.36 Encouragingly, rates of teen pregnancies have significantly decreased in recent years for all races and ethnicities in the United States.6,37 However, several groups with high teen pregnancy rates, (non-Hispanic Black women, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander women) also have the highest infant mortality rates, and prematurity rate and teen pregnancies are likely to play a factor in these outcomes. There are also significant regional differences in the United States in teen birth rates, with the Southern states having much higher rates of teen pregnancies.6,37
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: There has been great interest in the comparatively good infant mortality outcomes seen in Hispanics in the United States, despite many poor indicators of health care and overall health and high poverty. Interestingly, although teen pregnancies (ages
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: 15–19 years) are very high in Hispanic women,6 their rate of prematurity and infant mortality are similar to the rates seen in Non-Hispanic White women.2,6 Further research is needed to investigate the overall protective effect of Hispanic ethnicity on several infant outcomes. These findings are surprising given the noted poor access to prenatal care and low socioeconomic status for many of these Hispanic women. However, even in women who identify as Hispanic, there is a large variation in infant outcomes, with Puerto Rican infants having much higher mortality rates than other Hispanic infants.2 In addition, even within race and ethnicity there are likely additional factors not yet unidentified, because Hispanic women who identify as Black Hispanic have outcomes such as low birth weight, preterm birth, and small for gestational age intermediate of Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black women.38
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: Prematurity rates vary widely in the United States by state, with those in the Deep South and Appalachia, states with the highest percentage of non-Hispanic Black mothers or women with extreme poverty, showing the highest rates of prematurity and infant mortality (Fig. 8.5). These are also the states with the highest rates of preterm births.39 A recent CDC publication evaluated the maternal characteristics and infant outcomes in the United States, focusing on the Mississippi Delta and Appalachia. Women in the Delta were most likely to be teenagers, unmarried, and not have a college degree, followed by women in Appalachia, and then by women in the rest of the United States.40 Infants born in the Delta were more likely to be preterm (12.37%) or low birth weight (10.75%) and were more likely to die in their first year of life (8.17 infant deaths
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: per 1000 live births) than those born in Appalachia (10.75%, 8.87%, and 6.82%, respectively), whereas those born in the rest of the United States were the least likely.40
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: There are several short- and long-term morbidities associated with prematurity such as respiratory distress syndrome and chronic lung disease, infections, necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage, and abnormal long-term neurodevelopmental outcome. Several studies have revealed health disparities related to race and ethnicity in these morbidities. One study using a population-based retrospective cohort in New York City found significant racial and ethnic differences on neonatal morbidities for those infants born very preterm. In the fetuses-at-risk analysis, non-Hispanic Black infants had a 4.40-times higher rate of necrotizing enterocolitis, a 2.73times higher rate of intraventricular hemorrhage, a 4.43-times higher rate of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and a 2.98-times higher rate of retinopathy of prematurity. Hispanic infants had an approximately two times higher rate for all outcomes, and Asian infants had increased risk only for retinopathy of prematurity.41 In contrast, a study assessing whether racial/ ethnic disparities in major outcomes and key care practices were changing over time among extremely preterm infants in the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Neonatal Research Network born from 2006 to 2014 found an improvement in all outcomes over time and did not see a significant racial disparity in rate of improvement in outcomes. However, this study did not include premature infants that were Native American/Alaska Natives or Asia/Pacific Islanders.42 In addition, compared with the representation by race in the US
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: population, this study population was overrepresented with Black infants (cared for at level III-IV academic centers of excellence), which may not be representative of mortality and morbidity of Black infants when using a population sampling and the likelihood of many Black infants receiving neonatal intensive care at lower performing hospitals.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: As defined by the World Health Organization, the social determinants of health (SDOH) are the nonmedical factors that influence health outcomes. They are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age and the wider set of forces and systems shaping the conditions of daily life. These forces and systems include economic policies and systems, development agendas, social norms, social policies, and political systems.43 Health is determined in part by access to social and economic opportunities; the resources and supports available in homes, neighborhoods, and communities; the quality of schooling; the safety of workplaces; the cleanliness of water, food, and air; and the nature of social interactions and relationships. These circumstances are shaped by the distribution of money, power, and resources at global, national, and local levels. Health care disparities are important contributors to overall health disparities along with SDOH. These health care disparities adversely affect members of racial and ethnic minority groups and other socially disadvantaged populations. However, it is important to stress that “race” is not a biological entity but a socially defined group based on skin color or appearance. Thus it has become increasingly clear that there is no biologic predisposition to overall poor outcomes based on race but rather because of the inequities that are evident in the United States based on race and ethnicity.44 A discussion of maternal and infant health disparities would be incomplete without an exploration of these factors associated with health disparities.
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: These social determinants also greatly impact perinatal outcomes.45 SDOH have been described as largely responsible for the preventable differences in health status (health inequities). Poverty limits access to healthy foods and safe neighborhoods, and it is also known that increased education is a predictor of better health. A recent study found that a decrease in maternal education could explain persistent socioeconomic disparities in infant, neonatal, and postneonatal mortality rates in the United States.1 Examples of SDOH include: • Availability of resources to meet daily needs (e.g., safe
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: housing and local food markets) • Access to educational, economic, job opportunities, health
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: care services, and quality of education and job training • Availability of community-based resources in support of
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: community living and opportunities for recreational and leisure-time activities • Transportation options and public safety • Social support, social norms and attitudes (e.g., discrimi-
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: nation, racism, and distrust of government)
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: • Exposure to crime, violence, and social disorder (e.g.,
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: presence of trash and lack of cooperation in a community) • Socioeconomic conditions (e.g., concentrated poverty
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: and the stressful conditions that accompany it) • Residential segregation, language/literacy, and culture • Access to mass media and emerging technologies (e.g.,
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: cell phones, the Internet, and social media) A “place-based” organizing framework, reflecting five key areas of SDOH, was developed by Healthy People 2030.46 These five key areas (determinants) include: (1) economic stability, (2) education access and quality, (3) health care access and quality, (4) neighborhood and built environment, and (5) social and community context.46 Each of these five areas reflect several critical components/key issues that make up the underlying factors.
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: Recent emphasis has been placed on screening patients for the social determinants of health in the medical setting to improve health outcomes.47 Health literacy is considered an important social determinant of health that may underlie many health disparities, but it is possible that inadequate health literacy among pregnant individuals is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Inadequate maternal health literacy is associated with a variety of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes including a greater risk of cesarean delivery, small for gestational age, low birth weight, and a 5-minute Apgar score less than 4.48
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: The complex history of race and ethnicity in the United States may affect individual responses to medical recommendations for screening tests and adherence to treatment plans, contributing to disparate outcomes along racial lines. Numerous examples exist of racial and ethnic groups being targeted for forced medical procedures or experimentation. These past atrocities in the United States have left a lasting mistrust in minority communities. Although distrust of the health care system has not been well studied in the prenatal/obstetric/ neonatal context, it may be an important additional mediator in the relationship between utilization and outcomes for those at risk of disparities. Experiences of racism, segregation, and discrimination likely play a role in health system engagement and prenatal care utilization, as well as affecting the outcomes of premature infants.49 In a survey of mothers, non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic race/ethnicity was associated with almost three times higher odds of discrimination because of race, language, or culture, and uninsured women had nearly twice the odds of experiencing any perceived discrimination.50
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: Adequacy of prenatal care has been found to be significantly associated with improved infant outcomes, particularly gestational age at delivery and birth weight.50,51 Race6 and living in a distressed neighborhood are associated with late presentation to prenatal care. Proximity to the hospital is a key mediator in prenatal care utilization, and transportation to appointments and affordability of transportation are key factors in adherence to prenatal care. The impact of the neighborhood of residence on prenatal care disparities has not been explained by provider or physician supply alone. Racial segregation is likely to be an important factor in poorer outcomes seen by races and ethnicity. Mehra, investigating racial segregation based on maternal
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: residence at birth, found greater Black-White and Hispanic- White disparities in preterm birth in racially isolated counties (exposure) relative to nonisolated counties.52 However, they also found reduced Hispanic-White disparities in term low birth weight in racially concentrated and centralized counties relative to nonsegregated counties. Area-level poverty explained most of the moderating effect of segregation on disparities in adverse birth outcomes, suggesting that area-level poverty is a mediator of these associations. Segregation appears to modify racial/ethnic disparities in adverse birth outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: Social determinants such as insurance status, availability of social support in the form of childcare and adequate housing, neighborhood, and transportation likely play some role in prenatal care utilization and ultimately neonatal outcomes.50 Not surprisingly, a previous study investigating SDOH during a previous economic downturn in the United States indicated that individual and community indicators of need increased at these times.53 Providing adequate nutrition to mothers and infants via the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) program is an important assistance program in the United States. In this study, WIC may have been more effective at reducing late/no prenatal care utilization than the other maternal and child health safety net programs.53 Community-based research has shown that bundling prenatal care with other services such as child care that specifically aimed to reduce known disparities in social determinants improves outcomes.53 Homelessness in the United States has increased in recent years, also impacting those women of childbearing age. Non-Hispanic Black women are more likely to be homeless during their pregnancy or preconception period, and prenatal homelessness is associated with higher odds of low birth weight and preterm delivery. A recent study found homelessness in pregnancy was associated with adverse perinatal outcomes, including increased odds of preterm delivery across all gestational ages, and increased risk of NICU admission and low birth weight independent of preterm delivery.54
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: Access to health care is central to the delivery of health care services. In the health care context, it is defined as access to a service, a provider, or an institution, thus defined as the opportunity or ease with which consumers or communities are able to use appropriate services in proportion to their needs. Levesque et al.55 conceptualize five dimensions of accessibility of services: Approachability, Acceptability, Availability and Accommodation, Affordability, and Appropriateness. Five corresponding abilities of persons interact with these dimensions of accessibility to generate access; these dimensions of abilities include: Ability to perceive; Ability to seek; Ability to reach; Ability to pay; and Ability to engage. The various dimensions of access identified are not completely independent constructs.
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: Although the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) has increased the number of US children with coverage, insurance coverage alone does not guarantee access to needed health care. Angier et al. found affordability and lack of availability to be the most commonly reported barriers to health care access in a cohort of parents with incomes less than 133% of the federal poverty level; despite their child having health insurance, parents were unable to receive necessary health
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: care services.56 This is similar to reports from other studies highlighting lack of affordable and available care as major access barriers. Low socioeconomic status is associated with poor health status before, during, and after pregnancy.
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: The disturbing increases in racial and ethnic disparities in infant and neonatal mortality may be related to additional inequities in the provision of health care. Although the United States has always been a nation of immigrants, recent statelevel immigrant policies have made it much more difficult to address health inequities seen by race and ethnicity. Several states are seeking to criminalize immigrants, even those who are pregnant.57 A recent study analyzed birth record data from all 50 states and the District of Columbia in 2018, as well as state-level indicators of inclusive and criminalizing immigrant policies. More inclusive policies led to a reduction in preterm birth for those mothers born outside of the United States; in contrast, each additional criminalizing policy was associated with a 5% increase in preterm birth among Black women born outside the United States.57
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: Before the Affordable Care Act (ACA) spurred major expansions in health insurance coverage, non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic working-age adults were far more likely than non-Hispanic Whites to be uninsured.58 Uninsured women are 77% less likely to use obstetric services, have higher rates of severe morbidity, and are more likely to have inadequate prenatal care.50 Having health insurance makes it easier to gain access to and afford care, but insurance alone is unlikely to eliminate differences in access among all groups. Increased state-level Medicaid reimbursement for care increases adequate prenatal care utilization.
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: A recent systematic review by Sigurdson was performed to document racial/ethnic disparities in quality of care for infants in the NICU setting. Their review of more than 40 articles revealed complex racial and/or ethnic disparities in structure, process, and outcome measures, most often disadvantaging infants of color, especially non-Hispanic Black infants.59 Another study using the data from the Vermont Oxford Network (VON) found that infants were segregated among the 743 NICUs by race and ethnicity.60 Compared with non-Hispanic White infants, non-Hispanic Black infants were concentrated at NICUs with lower-quality scores, and Hispanic and Asian infants were concentrated at NICUs with higher-quality scores. Region of residence explained the observed inequality for Hispanic infants but not for non-Hispanic Black or Asian infants. There were large differences between geographic regions in NICU quality. Another study using the VON NICUs database examined care practices and outcomes, and relation to race and ethnicity over a 10-year period.61 Improvements in outcomes did occur, and compared with non-Hispanic White infants, non-Hispanic Black infants had a faster decline for mortality, hypothermia, necrotizing enterocolitis, and lateonset sepsis, whereas Hispanic infants had a faster decline for mortality, respiratory distress syndrome, and pneumothorax. However, despite the improvements, rate differences in outcomes including hypothermia, mortality, necrotizing enterocolitis, late onset sepsis, and severe intraventricular hemorrhage remained elevated by the end of the study period, especially
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: among non-Hispanic Black infants. Another study investigating unexpected newborn complication in New York City hospitals found non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic women were more likely to deliver in hospitals with high complication rates than were non-Hispanic White or Asian American women.62 The authors concluded these findings implicate hospital quality in contributing to preventable newborn health disparities among low-risk, term births. Nurse staffing and shortages may explain some of these continued disparities in NICUs. Survey data from a Multi-State Nursing Care and Patient Safety Study were analyzed and found nurses in high-Black NICUs missed nearly 50% more nursing care than in low-Black NICUs.63 Lower nurse staffing (an additional patient per nurse) significantly increased the odds of missed care, whereas better practice environments decreased the odds. Nurses in high-Black NICUs face inadequate staffing and they are more likely to miss required nursing care.
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: Racism, chronic stress, and worry by disadvantaged mothers likely have a significant impact on poor perinatal and neonatal outcomes. Braveman et al. found that non-Hispanic Black women reported significantly higher chronic worry about racial discrimination compared with non-Hispanic White women.64 Surprisingly, rates of worry for non-Hispanic Black women were highest in those with higher income and education levels. Those with the highest rates of worry also had the highest rates of preterm birth. Even more intriguing is the evidence for continued generational effects of racial disparities with non-Hispanic Black mothers who were small for gestational age or preterm themselves having a higher risk than non-Hispanic White mothers to deliver a subsequent small for gestational age or preterm infant.64a More recent studies have shown that pregnant women who are Hispanic or non-Hispanic Blacks experience frequent and pervasive discrimination and mistreatment during their pregnancy.65,66
paragraphs.heading: Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

paragraphs.text: It is unlikely that improving care in the NICU alone will have a dramatic impact on reducing the US neonatal and infant mortality rates. However, by addressing and improving the significant health disparities and racial and ethnic differences seen in outcomes, there can be marked improvements in this indicator of US population health. It is important to investigate the areas of greatest impact that will result in improving maternal and neonatal health, as well as which local, state, and national initiatives can result in significant improvements in outcomes. First, all women, but especially those at highest risk such as non-Hispanic Black women and Native American/Alaska women and Pacific Islanders, must have improved health status even before conception. Programs that can screen and identify women at risk must be implemented. Maternal and child health care must be easily accessible, affordable, and equitable for all. This is certainly a challenge in very rural/ remote areas where health care access is limited or nonexistent and mortality rates are higher compared with urban areas.67
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Access to adequate health care is also a challenge on most of the reservations and pueblos where many Native Americans reside. In addition, many urban settings have a maldistribution of health care providers and poor access to affordable transportation, making access difficult to those most in need.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: The causes of poor maternal health, including obesity, diabetes, and hypertension, are multifactorial, but chronic maternal stress related to racial and ethnic disparities seen in the United States may also play a significant role. Screening and health promotion for obesity, diabetes, and hypertension are critical to improving the health of the mother. Current models of physician reimbursement discourage the significant time needed for such interventions. Innovative models, such as mobile clinics, group counseling, and specially trained health care workers have all shown to improve health outcomes in women of childbearing age. Chronic conditions, such as hypertension and diabetes must be well controlled over time, with continued and affordable access to medications that are known to be effective. The current dramatic increase in obesity, especially in the South and among non-Hispanic Blacks, Native Americans, and Hispanics in the United States, is a particular challenge. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) has recently published Clinical Management Guidelines for the management of obesity in pregnancy.68 This guideline offers an integrated approach to the management of obesity in women of reproductive age who are planning a pregnancy because of the concern for adverse outcomes. It also acknowledges the difficulty in successfully treating obesity in this population. Not often recognized is the lack of healthy food available in underserved and rural areas, as well as urban food deserts, which contributes to this problem. Similar to obesity management, mothers must be screened and treated for diabetes, hypertension, and renal disease before and during pregnancy. This will reduce many of the adverse outcomes seen in neonates and infants.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Other modifiable factors must be addressed for women at risk of becoming pregnant. Tobacco, alcohol, narcotics, and illicit substance use/abuse all have negative impacts on pregnancy outcomes and are often disproportionately used by those at highest risk of adverse outcomes. Culturally specific and appropriate educational materials and interventions must be available in a variety of settings, including schools. Tobacco cessation programs specifically during pregnancy, especially quitting early in pregnancy, have been shown to decrease the risk of preterm birth, especially if cessation occurs prior to conception.69 Alcohol use and abuse is particularly high among Native American and Alaska Natives and results in high rates of fetal alcohol syndrome.70 Fetal alcohol syndrome/fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is the largest cause of preventable long-term neurodevelopmental disability in children. Treatment of those ingesting alcohol during pregnancy is particularly difficult. However, intensive interventions have made some impact.71 Finally, the current opioid epidemic has been well publicized, as has the impact on those at the lowest socioeconomic populations. Pregnant women are often the least likely to get medical help given the highly punitive
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: nature of some state programs, even to the point of arresting and incarcerating pregnant women, especially those women of minorities. However, programs that deal with multiple aspects of maternal drug use with known effective interventions and a less punitive approach have been shown to significantly improve neonatal and maternal outcomes, including more controlled or even cessation of drug use.72 Other innovative prenatal care programs such as group-based centering, easier access to care during pregnancy, and culturally centered care models also have been shown to have a significant impact on avoiding adverse outcomes of pregnancy.73
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Renewed efforts must be made to improve the prepregnancy health of the mother. An important factor is access to health care and health insurance. Medicaid provides health insurance to those poorest Americans including the “working poor,” but this coverage is still woefully inadequate. Recent efforts have been made by the federal government to expand Medicaid coverage, but many states with significant minority populations, as well as eligible non-Hispanic Whites, have declined to expand eligibility for their Medicaid programs. Recent federal initiatives to provide even greater incentives to states have been only partially successful. Adults in Medicaid expansion states reported better coverage and access rates, narrower disparities between groups, and greater improvements across nearly every measure between 2013 and 2019.74 Interestingly, Hispanic adults continue to have the highest percentage of uninsured population, perhaps a reflection of concerns about immigration status/noncitizenship and subsequent adverse consequences of accessing the medical system. The most recent years since 2016 have seen a further deterioration in Medicaid coverage for all those in the United States, especially for Hispanics and non-Hispanic Blacks.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Access to insurance coverage before, during, and after pregnancy is also a vital piece of health care and improving maternal and infant outcomes. Having health insurance reduces racial and ethnic disparities in key measures of pregnancy for health care access and affordability, even after adjusting for income and other factors. Medicaid is currently the largest payor for maternity care in the United States. Implementation of the ACA and Medicaid expansion has decreased racial and ethnic disparities in insurance and access, and more quality-of-care measures are improving than worsening for racial and ethnic minority groups. However, many disparities have not changed, and overall progress is modest.75 Based on data from 2011 to 2016, state Medicaid expansion was not significantly associated with differences in rates of low birth weight or preterm birth outcomes overall, although there were significant improvements in relative disparities for non-Hispanic Black infants compared with for non-Hispanic White infants in states that expanded Medicaid versus those that did not.75 In contrast, a study by Bhatt did show that overall infant mortality rate decline was greater in Medicaid expansion states, with greater declines among non-Hispanic Black infants.76 Recent data indicate that insurance source can impact neonatal outcomes. A study by Kim et al. looked at infant mortality by payment source for delivery in the United States. They found overall infant mortality was lower in mothers who paid with private
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: insurance than in those who paid with Medicaid insurance (relative risk [RR] = 0.91 in 2017), but it was higher in self-paid women than in Medicaid-insured women at delivery (RR = 1.16, in 2017). Non-Hispanic Black (RR = 1.16 in 2017) and Hispanic (RR = 1.22 in 2017) mothers with self-payment had a higher risk for infant mortality than those with Medicaid at delivery. They found newborns whose mothers have no health insurance are more vulnerable to infant mortality than Medicaid beneficiaries, and non-Hispanic White ethnic groups with self-payment have an elevated risk of infant mortality among other racial and ethnic groups.77
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: As noted earlier, the ACA has significantly decreased the uninsured in the United States, with varying improvements based on states’ Medicaid expansion. This program has also mandated insurance coverage by all health plans for prenatal, postnatal, and infant care. Nonetheless, minority women and children in the United States are still less likely to be insured. The CHIP funded by the United States has increased coverage of uninsured children. Survey-based research shows positive associations between CHIP expansions and children’s health care utilization. Thus continued access to insurance for women and children is likely to have a significant impact on reducing the disparities seen in health outcomes in the United States. Unlike other developed countries, the United States has no universal health care, and the ACA has been a significant, albeit controversial, improvement in this area. Those in health care, both providers and insurers, must advocate for the most vulnerable in the population to maintain and expand this coverage.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Women often qualify for Medicaid coverage once the pregnancy is identified but cannot access the health care system before the pregnancy to improve their health, thus putting them at greater risk. Medicaid coverage increases during pregnancy for those mothers that are noninsured or underinsured. Recent federal efforts have also focused on increasing current postpartum coverage from 6 weeks to 12 months to improve the care of the mother while her child is young and for the next pregnancy. Data for new mothers with Medicaidcovered prenatal care in 2015 to 2018 from 43 states participating in the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) found that 26.8% of new mothers with Medicaid-covered prenatal care were uninsured before pregnancy, 21.9% became uninsured 2 to 6 months postpartum, and 34.5% were uninsured in either period, with higher perinatal uninsurance rates in nonexpansion states and for Hispanic women who completed the PRAMS survey in Spanish.78 Together, these findings indicate that, despite recent coverage gains, further policy change is needed to help women maintain health insurance coverage before and after pregnancy and to allow them to address ongoing health issues including obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and depression. Again, many states have been resistant to implementing this expanded coverage despite federal support. Only half of the states have implemented or plan to implement expanded postpartum coverage. Of concern is that some of the states with the greatest racial perinatal disparities or worst perinatal outcomes are those that have resisted expanded postpartum coverage for up
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: to 12 months.79 However, studies have shown that mothers at greatest health inequities may still have significant medical issues such as hypertension at 6 weeks postpartum, at which time they may no longer be eligible for Medicaid coverage.80
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: In addition, improving nutrition for women and infants can have a significant impact on outcome. A recent study examined the association between race and ethnicity, participation in WIC, and a series of infant health outcomes including infant mortality, low birth weight, preterm birth, extended infant hospitalization, and stays in the NICU.81 In this study, using the PRAMS from 2009 to 2017, infants born to non-Hispanic Black women, and to a lesser extent Hispanic women, were in worse health than those born to non-Hispanic White mothers in the United States. However, participation in WIC was associated with reductions in the gap in infant health experienced by racial and ethnic minorities. They concluded prenatal WIC participation was associated with improvements in the health of non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic infants and reduced racial and ethnic disparities in infant health outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Another public health initiative which will have a significant impact on health care disparities in the perinatal and neonatal period is in pregnancy delay, short interpregnancy intervals, and prevention of unintended pregnancies. Improved education about pregnancy prevention, including in the schools, as well as easier access to contraception, is critical. In addition, long-acting reproductive contraception (LARC) has been shown to be particularly effective and is reversible at the time of desired pregnancy. Contraception for those who desire it must be more readily available, especially immediately after delivery of a baby. Contraceptive counseling is rarely done during postpartum care or while a baby is in the NICU, but these are valuable missed opportunities to improve the health of the mother and her future children. Improved access to contraception will also increase interpregnancy intervals. Short interpregnancy intervals less than 6 months are more common in non-Hispanic Black mothers (7.1%) compared with non-Hispanic White mothers (4.1%) and Hispanic mothers (5.0%).82 The shortest interval of interpregnancy conception (<6 months) has been shown to have the highest adverse outcomes, especially in teen mothers.83 Access to contraception, especially for teen pregnancies, of which three-fourths are unintended, is critical to lengthen interpregnancy intervals and prevent adverse outcomes associated with teen pregnancy. Local legislation will be important to this public health intervention. For unwanted pregnancies, or for women that feel they cannot support having another child, abortion is an option. However, many states are considering or have implemented restrictions on abortion, especially those states with high minority populations. In addition, there are racial disparities in abortion rates for women of lower socioeconomic status and women of color. Hispanic women and non-Hispanic Black women have an up to fourfold higher rate of abortion than non-Hispanic White women.84 Recent efforts to decrease access to abortion for these women may only widen the health disparities for future generations.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: As noted earlier, there are significant disparities in rates of prenatal care related to race and ethnicity, with non- Hispanic Blacks overall having the lowest rates of adequate
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: prenatal care and the highest rates of no prenatal care (see Table 8.1). Innovative models must be investigated and implemented. Statewide Medicaid-enhanced prenatal care programs have been shown to reduce infant mortality risk.85 Implementation of such a program in Michigan reduced the odds of infant death by 27%, with the highest reduction in Black infant mortality (29%). The greatest reduction was seen in those women who fully participated in the program using a population-based home visitation program to improve outcomes. For non-Hispanic Black women, this program further resulted in lower odds of low birth weight (0.76), very low birth weight (0.42), and very preterm birth (0.41) compared with matched nonparticipants.86
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Although the underlying cause of prematurity is multifactorial and not clearly understood, certain interventions have been shown to reduce preterm birth. For those women identified with a singleton pregnancy and a previous history of spontaneous preterm birth, 17 alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17P) has been shown to reduce the risk of subsequent preterm delivery by up to 30%.87 However, access to this medication requires weekly injections, and the current drug delivery and reimbursement model is problematic for both physicians and women at risk. Many state Medicaid plans are investigating novel methods to deliver this drug to mothers at risk, given its known effectiveness.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: Breastfeeding has been shown to have important benefits to both the mother and infant, including decreased breast and ovarian cancer rates and less postpartum depression and osteoporosis in the mother, as well as fewer infections, less risk of diabetes, heart disease, and asthma in the infant. Breastfeeding also has a significant impact on infant mortality. More importantly, breastfeeding initiation is significantly associated with reduced odds of post-perinatal infant death in multiple racial and ethnic groups within the US population.88 However, significant disparities exist in the rates of breastfeeding among different races and ethnicities.89 Non-Hispanic Black women have the lowest rates of initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding at 6 months, and any breastfeeding at 12 months. The disparities in adjusted breastfeeding rates have also become larger between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White infants in recent years. In addition, certain areas of the United States with the highest poverty levels, such as the Deep South and Appalachian states, have the lowest rates of breastfeeding. However, targeted interventions can be successful in improving breastfeeding rates in this part of the United States. After implementing the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding program in delivery hospitals in four Southern states, the disparity in breastfeeding initiation between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White infants decreased by 9.6% over the course of 31 months.90 Breastfeeding initiation increased from 66% to 75% for all races combined, and exclusivity increased from 34% to 39%. Initiation and exclusive breastfeeding among non-Hispanic Black infants increased from 46% to 63% and from 19% to 31%, respectively. Successful implementation of breastfeeding must begin before delivery with targeted and appropriate education. Baby-friendly initiatives in the United States have resulted in increased awareness of the importance of this public health
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: measure, but more must be done. Lactation specialists must be available to all mothers immediately after delivery and during the postnatal period to improve initiation of and adherence to breastfeeding. Finally, the United States has no national policy guaranteeing paid leave to employed women who give birth, one of only three countries worldwide.91 Paid maternity leave significantly predicts lower odds of maternal and infant rehospitalization and higher odds of doing well with exercise and stress management. Paid maternity leave also promotes breastfeeding for a longer period of time with increased benefit to the infant and mother.
paragraphs.heading: Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

paragraphs.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and March of Dimes (MOD) have initiated the Safe Sleep campaign in an effort to reduce SIDS.92 Of concern is the current increase in SUID/SIDS and accidental strangulation in bed in the United States noted in some states. Although the Safe Sleep program is effective, other measures must be addressed, such as the lack of separate sleeping spaces for the infant and cobedding in minority populations. It is often difficult to intervene in those families with limited finances. Programs such as Back to Sleep and Baby Sleeping Boxes are simple and effective interventions. However, continued local and state educational efforts must be maintained and supported.

paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: Finally, improving the overall health and economic status of those most disadvantaged in the United States will result in improved perinatal and neonatal/infant outcomes. Implementation of measures such as increased educational opportunities, job creation, and statewide early intervention programs are beyond the scope of this chapter. However, some of the interventions to address these issues have been shown to be beneficial in other countries. Canada implemented unconditional prenatal income supplements to mothers already receiving prenatal social assistance and observed reductions in low birth weight (21%) and preterm births (17.5%) and increases in breastfeeding.94 It is important to note that continued accurate data collection by the CDC regarding maternal, perinatal, infant, and neonatal measures, in particular as they relate to perinatal and neonatal health disparities in the United States, will be critical to monitoring outcomes and future improvements in mortality and morbidity. Every baby deserves a first birthday. Effective interventions exist that will help more to reach this goal.

8 Social and Economic Contributors to Neonatal Outcome in the United States

### RENATE D. SAVICH AND MOBOLAJI FAMUYIDE

### Epidemiology of Health Disparities in Neonatal and Perinatal Medicine

Although there have been significant improvements in infant mortality (death within 1 year of life) and neonatal mortality (death within 28 days of life) in the United States over the past 50 years, compared with other highincome countries in the world, the United States alarmingly lags behind these other countries in infant mortality rates.1 Infant mortality and morbidity rates are commonly used as an important indicator worldwide of overall population health. Recent research has focused on why the United States has not seen continued improvements in these public health indices as have other countries, and indeed several markers of US infant health have worsened in recent years. It is important to understand recent US trends and contributing factors to provide optimal care and public health planning in the prenatal, perinatal, neonatal, and postneonatal periods to improve these outcomes. One major factor contributing to these poor perinatal and infant outcomes in the United States is the significant health disparities seen among women and infants related to race and ethnicity. Other disparities in health outcomes in the perinatal and infant period in the United States are related to poverty, poor maternal health, lack of health care access and health insurance, and other overall indicators of poor socioeconomic status.

### Infant Mortality

Although the United States had a steady decline in infant mortality over the past decades, declining 19% from 6.89 deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 5.58 per 1000 in 2019

(Fig. 8.1),2 this rate is still almost twice that of other comparable countries in the world. Recent data comparing infant mortality indicated that the United States had two to three times the infant mortality rate of countries such as Japan, Italy, and Sweden1 in spite of significantly larger health care expenditures in the United States per capita compared with these other countries.3 Multiple studies have attempted to delineate the factors unique to the United States that might explain this discrepancy. The United States has made continued progress in decreasing the neonatal mortality rate as well, with a rate of 3.69 per 1000 births in 2019, a significant decrease from 4.62 per 1000 births documented in 2000.2 However, this rate is also significantly higher than the neonatal mortality rates seen in comparable countries.

Prematurity (infants born at less than 37 weeks) overall in the United States has a major impact on the high infant mortality rates. Previous studies show that the United States has rates of prematurity two to three times that of other developed countries.4 Clearly this is a significant contributor to the high infant mortality seen in the United States. During the 1990s and early 2000s, the US preterm birth rate steadily increased by 20% from 10.6% in 1990 to 12.8% in 2006.5 At that time, after widespread public health efforts, it seemed the United States was making significant progress in decreasing the rate of prematurity. The United States initially saw a steady decrease in the prematurity rate over the next decade, with a decrease to 9.57% in 2014, the lowest rate the United States has ever experienced (Fig. 8.2).6 Disturbingly, this trend in the prematurity rate has reversed in recent years, with a significant increase in the younger than 37 weeks’ birthrate to 10.23% in 2019 and 10.09% in 2020, primarily because of an increase in late preterm births (34–36 weeks’ completed gestation).6,7 It is unclear

Given that the percentage overall of preterm births in the United States is twice that of comparable countries, addressing the causes of prematurity are critical to reducing the US infant mortality rate. However, a higher rate of prematurity alone does not explain the higher US infant mortality rate because the gestational age specific infant mortality rates are also increased above other countries at gestational ages 32 weeks and greater, the category with the highest number of preterm births as well as term births.4,6 Addressing prematurity is a significant financial priority as well as public health priority. Recent estimates from a large commercially insured population (763,566 infants) reveal that the cost for the median term birth for the first 6 months of life was $3787, whereas for a premature infant born at 24 weeks, the median cost for the first 6 months is $548,865.8 It was estimated that in recent years, more than $25 billion is spent each year on premature births.9
