As noted, overall infant mortality rates in total and for each race or ethnic group have decreased each year.2,11 It appeared that the United States was making great strides in reducing the discrepancies in infant mortality rates related to race with a 20% decline from 2005 to 2014 seen in non-Hispanic Black rates compared to the overall US decline of 16% during those years. However, recent US infant mortality data show disturbingly that in 2019, only non-Hispanic Whites had a significant decrease; other groups did not show a statistically significant improvement.2 Of concern, the 2019 data indicate that for non-Hispanic Black infants compared to non-Hispanic White infants, the infant mortality rate disparity increased from 2.24 in 2014 to 2.37 in 2019. The disparity in neonatal mortality for non-Hispanic Black infants compared to non-Hispanic White infants also is disturbingly high at 2.35. However, a different picture emerges for neonatal and infant mortality rates of Native American/Alaska Natives and Native Hawaiian/ Pacific Islanders. These two groups have also had higher infant mortality rates compared to non-Hispanic White infants (see Fig. 8.3). However, for both non-Hispanic White and Black infants the contribution to infant mortality of deaths for the postneonatal period is similar at about 35%, while for Pacific Islanders it is increased to almost 40% of infant mortality and for American Indian or Alaska Native infants, the contribution to infant mortality in the postneonatal period is almost 50%.2 Thus it is likely that there are differences in each of these racial groups for the higher infant mortality rates compared to non-Hispanic White infants and it appears that in the United States, these disparities by race are worsening in recent years. As noted, infant mortality rates for Hispanics track closely with those of non-Hispanic White infants. Interestingly, when looking closely at the infant and neonatal mortality rates in Hispanics by ethnicity, wide ranges exist, with Cuban Hispanic infants having a much lower infant mortality rate compared to Puerto Rican Hispanic infants in 2019 (4.14 per 1,000 live births compared to 6.17 per 1,000 live births.2 In addition, there are significant differences in infant mortality by state in the United States, with the southern states having the highest infant mortality. These are also the states with the highest percentage of non-Hispanic Black women in their population (Fig. 8.4). In addition, those states with the greatest increase in level of income inequality in recent years have higher risks of infant and neonatal mortality.12

It is also important to evaluate perinatal mortality rates (late fetal deaths at 28 completed weeks of gestation or more and early neonatal deaths less than age 7 days) because this can be an indicator of the quality of health care before, during, and after delivery and also of the health status of the nation. In addition, late fetal deaths are not accounted for in neonatal and infant mortality and may skew infant mortality rates when evaluating by race. Similar to infant mortality in

the United States, there was a significant decrease in perinatal mortality in the United States from 1990 to 2011, which did not improve over the next 5 years. Encouragingly, there has been a small but significant decrease in perinatal mortality since 2017 in both late fetal and early neonatal deaths.13 However, mirroring the infant mortality rate disparities, fetal deaths and perinatal mortality rates show wide ranges when looking closely at race and ethnicity. Non-Hispanic Black fetal mortality rates are twice as high as non-Hispanic White rates.13 Poorer maternal health and decreased access to prenatal care may have an impact on this outcome.

To understand the impact of race and ethnicity on neonatal and infant mortality in the United States, we must first understand whether differences exist in maternal and prenatal factors that would impact mortality. Similar to the significant racial disparities seen in infant mortality, the incidence of prematurity (babies less than 37 weeks) varies greatly by race and ethnicity. Non-Hispanic Black women consistently have the highest rate of overall prematurity, and it was almost 60% higher than the prematurity rates of non-Hispanic White women in 2020.6 The disparities in the incidence of severe prematurity also increase greatly by race and ethnicity, with the percentage of births less than 28 weeks (the risk of highest mortality) in 2020 for non-Hispanic Blacks being more than three times the percent of non-Hispanic Whites in 2020 (1.47% vs. 0.44%).6 When evaluating the impact of prematurity on mortality, those born at the lowest gestational ages have the highest mortality. Similar to infant mortality outcomes, the highest prematurity rate of infants born less than 34 weeks occurs for non-Hispanic Black infants (4.82 %) compared with non-Hispanic Whites (2.21%). The lowest prematurity rate of infants less than 34 weeks is seen in Asian infants (2.08%), with Hispanic infants (2.52%) slightly greater than those of non-Hispanic Whites (Table 8.1). American Indian/Alaskan Native infants and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander infants show a more favorable less than 34-week percentage at 3.05% and 3.08% of births, respectively, in 2020 compared with the rate for non-Hispanic Black infants.6 As noted previously, overall US prematurity rates for less than 37 weeks’ gestation are increased in recent years compared with the lowest rate in 2014, and we will need to carefully investigate the contribution of racial disparities to this recent increase in prematurity.6,7 Similar to the wide variation in infant mortality by state in the United States, there are vast differences state by state in the rate of prematurity in the United States, with Southern states having the highest preterm rates (see Fig. 8.4).

The five leading causes of infant mortality in the United States are congenital malformations, short gestation and low birth weight, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) or sudden unexpected infant death (SUID), unintentional injuries, and maternal complications.2 Recent data show that these causes of death vary in importance and impact by racial and ethnic group. Congenital malformations are the leading cause of death for non-Hispanic White infants,2 whereas death because of low birth weight/preterm-related causes is the leading cause of death for non-Hispanic Blacks compared with non-Hispanic

Similar racial disparities for American Indian or Alaska Natives are seen in SUID. For American Indian or Alaska Natives, the largest difference in mortality outcomes when compared with non- Hispanic Whites is the twofold increase in deaths caused by SUID (American Indian: 177.6 per 100,000 live births, non-Hispanic White: 84.5 per 100,000 live births).17 Non- Hispanic Blacks also have an extremely high rate of mortality from SUID (172.4 per 100,000 live births), only slightly lower than the rate for Native American infants.17 The lowest rate of SUID is seen in Hispanic and Asian/Pacific Islander infants (Hispanic: 49.3 per 100,000 live births, Asian/Pacific Islanders: 28.3 per 100,000 live births), even lower than the non-Hispanic White rate. A significant impact on SUID is decreasing gestational age at birth, with infants born at 24 to 27 weeks having a 3.5- to 5-fold increase in the rate of SIDS compared with term infants.18 Again, racial disparities are seen here, with a SUID rate in non-Hispanic Blacks at less than 28 weeks of 382.3 per 100,000 live births compared with the lowest group Asian/Pacific Islanders: 126.6 per 100,000 live births at less than 28 weeks.17 Given that the highest rate of prematurity is seen in non-Hispanic Blacks, this contribution to SIDS/SUID also negatively impacts this population and infant mortality. It is unclear what impact genetic versus cultural factors may play in mortality caused by SUID and SIDS. Finally, there has been a distressing increase in infant mortality because of accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed (ASSB) over more than 20 years.19 A recent study has shown that ASSB mortality continues to increase significantly: for 1999 to 2016, 4.4-fold for non-Hispanic Black girls (45.8 per 100,000 in 2016), 3.5-fold for non-Hispanic Black boys (53.8), 2.7-fold for non-Hispanic White girls (15.8), and 4.0-fold for non-Hispanic White boys (25.9). As for many other factors impacting the racial inequities impacting infant mortality, the overall rates were much higher for non-Hispanic Black infants. The authors also noted factors previously associated with ASSB (unmarried mothers and mothers with low educational attainment, low infant birth weight, low gestational age, lack of prenatal care) continue to be associated with both overall ASSB and racial inequalities adversely affecting non-Hispanic Black infants.

### Maternal Mortality

Maternal mortality related to pregnancy has been steadily increasing in the United States over the past 20 years and

continues to increase20,21 despite significant decreases seen in other high-income countries during this same time period.

A maternal death is defined by the World Health Organization as “the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and the site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.” Again, alarming racial and ethnic disparities are seen in pregnancy-related mortality in the United States, with non-Hispanic Black women dying at a rate almost three times that of non-Hispanic White women (55.3/100,000 live births vs. 19.1/100,000).20 This is especially concerning for pregnant non-Hispanic Black women over the age of 40, with a rate of 263.1 per 100,000 live births.20 The higher maternal mortality rates for Black women are consistent regardless of education level.22 For Native American and Alaska Natives mothers, similar to the high infant mortality rates, the maternal mortality rates are more than twice that of non-Hispanic White mothers.22 Maternal mortality rates have also increased over the past years for Hispanic mothers, but their rates are similar to, and even slightly lower than, non-Hispanic White mothers.22 Although the reasons for the dramatic increase in US pregnancy related mortality and morbidity are not clearly understood, underlying poorer maternal health, obesity, lack of prenatal care, poor access to medical care, inadequate or no health insurance, teen pregnancies, and single mothers without support systems all are likely contributors to this high mortality rate. Maternal morbidities and other indicators of poor health care during pregnancy are significantly higher in non-Hispanic Black women and American Indian and Alaskan Native women compared with Non-Hispanic White women.6,23,24 Maternal deaths caused by hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, emboli, and anesthesia complications have declined because of state initiatives and focused educational and obstetric interventions; however, contributions to maternal death from cardiovascular conditions, cardiomyopathy, stroke, and noncardiovascular medical conditions have significantly increased in recent years.24 Looking more closely at severe maternal morbidity during the delivery period and post delivery in the Medicaid population, non- Hispanic Black women (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.53), Hispanic women (aOR, 1.46), and women of other races or ethnicities (aOR, 1.40) had higher rates of morbidity during delivery hospitalization than non-Hispanic White women; however, only the disparity between Black and White women (aOR, 1.69; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.57–1.81) persisted into the postdischarge period.23 Racial disparities impact a variety of maternal morbidities, with non-Hispanic Black and American Indian and Alaska Native women having the highest rates of blood transfusion, heart failure, shock, eclampsia, and renal failure in the perinatal period, as well as an overall rate of severe maternal morbidity more than twice that of non- Hispanic White women during delivery hospitalization.24 Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are particularly dangerous conditions leading to maternal morbidity and death, as well as several neonatal complications, especially preterm birth and its associated complications for the neonate. The rates of


## PDF page 157

hypertensive disorders of pregnancy as well as chronic hypertension in women during their pregnancies have dramatically increased in the past 30 years.25 Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are highest in non-Hispanic Black mothers and American Indians/Alaska Natives but lower in Hispanics and Asians compared with non-Hispanic White women.26 However, in a study looking at more than 11 million deliveries in the United States from 2016 to 2018, although Black women were the most likely to experience preeclampsia, Asian/Pacific women were the most at risk for acute cardiovascular complications during delivery hospitalization.26 In addition, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and subsequent elective deliveries because of maternal risks are a leading cause of prematurity.

As noted, the worsening health of many women before and during pregnancy has been a leading cause of poor maternal and infant outcomes.25 The massive rise in obesity in the US population over the past years has been well documented. Of significant concern to those in the public health arena is how this has negatively impacted women of productive age and their future children. Maternal obesity is another aspect of health disparities in that those races and ethnicities exhibiting worse perinatal and neonatal outcomes also have significantly higher rates of obesity than the general population. Recent data indicate that in the past decade, non-Hispanic Black women older than the ages of 20 have an extremely high incidence of obesity at 56.9% compared with non-Hispanic White women at 39.8%.27 Hispanic women also suffer from this epidemic of increased weight with a recent obesity incidence of 43.7%. In recent years, the rate of prepregnancy obesity has increased significantly in spite of the known health risks during pregnancy. Disparities in the incidence of obesity during pregnancy also are seen in non-Hispanic Black women who have the highest rates of obesity before and during pregnancy in the general population, especially at the highest categories of obesity. From 2016 to 2019, the percentage of non-Hispanic White women with prepregnancy obesity rose 10% (from 24.1% to 26.6%), 7% for non-Hispanic Black women (36.4%–39.1%), and 12% for Hispanic women (28.9%–32.4%).28 Obesity is known to increase the risk of gestational diabetes from a baseline of 2.8% to a high of 14.6% in pregnant women with class III obesity.29 Other morbidities of pregnancy such as gestational hypertensive disorders (increasing fourfold at highest obesity classes), infection, cesarean section rates, and cardiovascular events are all higher in obese pregnant women. Although obesity has its own risks of increased morbidity in pregnant women, obesity is also associated with increased neonatal/infant mortality and morbidity, as well as preterm delivery and congenital malformations.28 Infant mortality increases with each increase in obesity category. Declercq et al. found that with a normal prepregnancy weight as a reference, the odds ratio (OR) for an infant death rose from 1.32 for mothers in the obese I category up to 1.73 for obese III category pregnant mothers.30 Lemon et al. reported that compared with non-Hispanic White women, non-Hispanic Black women were more likely to have obesity and experienced a higher rate of stillbirth (8.3 vs. 3.6 stillbirths per 1000 liveborn and stillborn infants) and infant death (8.5 vs. 3.0 infant deaths per 1000 live births).31

In addition, obesity during pregnancy also is associated with increased neonatal morbidities such as increased prematurity, sepsis, large for gestational age infants, and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission.29 Increasing obesity also results in an increased risk of major malformations in the neonate and were the highest as the severity of obesity increased.32 Congenital malformations were seen in the cardiovascular system, malformations of the nervous system, and limb defects. Clearly, the obesity epidemic is adversely affecting minority women during pregnancy and their babies disproportionately. It is also likely that an impact to reduce these adverse outcomes must be implemented before conception to impact these events which develop even before most mothers realize they are pregnant.

Separate from its relation to obesity, there has also been a significant increase in diabetes during pregnancy, both for type I and II diabetes before pregnancy and gestational diabetes during pregnancy.25,33 Diabetes during pregnancy leads to significant poor outcomes for the mother, as well as for the fetus and infant. Severe maternal diabetes at the time of conception can result in major congenital anomalies. Diabetes during the pregnancy can result in cardiac anomalies, birth asphyxia, and severe hypoglycemia in the neonate. However, there are known racial and ethnic differences in gestational diabetes. A recent study of gestational diabetes by Shah et al. found that, among individuals with a singleton first live birth in the United States from 2011 to 2019, rates of gestational diabetes increased across all racial and ethnic subgroups, overall by 3.7% per year. Gestational diabetes rates were highest in Asian Indian mothers, and among Hispanic/Latina participants, gestational diabetes rates were highest among Puerto Rican individuals.33 However, this study did not include American Indians/Alaska Natives, a group known to have extremely high rates of both pre-existing diabetes and gestational diabetes.34 In addition, this study also found that non- Hispanic Black mothers had the highest rate of pregestational diabetes, more than 50% higher than non-Hispanic White mothers (14.2 per 1000 live births compared with 7.9).33

A significant body of research has focused on the high teen pregnancy rate in the United States compared with other high-income countries. ### Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

As defined by the World Health Organization, the social determinants of health (SDOH) are the nonmedical factors that influence health outcomes. They are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age and the wider set of forces and systems shaping the conditions of daily life. These forces and systems include economic policies and systems, development agendas, social norms, social policies, and political systems.43 Health is determined in part by access to social and economic opportunities; the resources and supports available in homes, neighborhoods, and communities; the quality of schooling; the safety of workplaces; the cleanliness of water, food, and air; and the nature of social interactions and relationships. These circumstances are shaped by the distribution of money, power, and resources at global, national, and local levels. Health care disparities are important contributors to overall health disparities along with SDOH. These health care disparities adversely affect members of racial and ethnic minority groups and other socially disadvantaged populations. However, it is important to stress that “race” is not a biological entity but a socially defined group based on skin color or appearance. Thus it has become increasingly clear that there is no biologic predisposition to overall poor outcomes based on race but rather because of the inequities that are evident in the United States based on race and ethnicity.44 A discussion of maternal and infant health disparities would be incomplete without an exploration of these factors associated with health disparities.

These social determinants also greatly impact perinatal outcomes.45 SDOH have been described as largely responsible for the preventable differences in health status (health inequities). Poverty limits access to healthy foods and safe neighborhoods, and it is also known that increased education is a predictor of better health. A recent study found that a decrease in maternal education could explain persistent socioeconomic disparities in infant, neonatal, and postneonatal mortality rates in the United States.1 Examples of SDOH include: • Availability of resources to meet daily needs (e.g., safe

housing and local food markets) • Access to educational, economic, job opportunities, health

community living and opportunities for recreational and leisure-time activities • Transportation options and public safety • Social support, social norms and attitudes (e.g., discrimi-

and the stressful conditions that accompany it) • Residential segregation, language/literacy, and culture • Access to mass media and emerging technologies (e.g.,

cell phones, the Internet, and social media) A “place-based” organizing framework, reflecting five key areas of SDOH, was developed by Healthy People 2030.46 These five key areas (determinants) include: (1) economic stability, (2) education access and quality, (3) health care access and quality, (4) neighborhood and built environment, and (5) social and community context.46 Each of these five areas reflect several critical components/key issues that make up the underlying factors.

Recent emphasis has been placed on screening patients for the social determinants of health in the medical setting to improve health outcomes.47 Health literacy is considered an important social determinant of health that may underlie many health disparities, but it is possible that inadequate health literacy among pregnant individuals is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Inadequate maternal health literacy is associated with a variety of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes including a greater risk of cesarean delivery, small for gestational age, low birth weight, and a 5-minute Apgar score less than 4.48

The complex history of race and ethnicity in the United States may affect individual responses to medical recommendations for screening tests and adherence to treatment plans, contributing to disparate outcomes along racial lines. Numerous examples exist of racial and ethnic groups being targeted for forced medical procedures or experimentation. These past atrocities in the United States have left a lasting mistrust in minority communities. Although distrust of the health care system has not been well studied in the prenatal/obstetric/ neonatal context, it may be an important additional mediator in the relationship between utilization and outcomes for those at risk of disparities. Experiences of racism, segregation, and discrimination likely play a role in health system engagement and prenatal care utilization, as well as affecting the outcomes of premature infants.49 In a survey of mothers, non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic race/ethnicity was associated with almost three times higher odds of discrimination because of race, language, or culture, and uninsured women had nearly twice the odds of experiencing any perceived discrimination.50

Adequacy of prenatal care has been found to be significantly associated with improved infant outcomes, particularly gestational age at delivery and birth weight.50,51 Race6 and living in a distressed neighborhood are associated with late presentation to prenatal care. Proximity to the hospital is a key mediator in prenatal care utilization, and transportation to appointments and affordability of transportation are key factors in adherence to prenatal care. The impact of the neighborhood of residence on prenatal care disparities has not been explained by provider or physician supply alone. Racial segregation is likely to be an important factor in poorer outcomes seen by races and ethnicity. Mehra, investigating racial segregation based on maternal

Access to health care is central to the delivery of health care services. In the health care context, it is defined as access to a service, a provider, or an institution, thus defined as the opportunity or ease with which consumers or communities are able to use appropriate services in proportion to their needs. Levesque et al.55 conceptualize five dimensions of accessibility of services: Approachability, Acceptability, Availability and Accommodation, Affordability, and Appropriateness. Five corresponding abilities of persons interact with these dimensions of accessibility to generate access; these dimensions of abilities include: Ability to perceive; Ability to seek; Ability to reach; Ability to pay; and Ability to engage. The various dimensions of access identified are not completely independent constructs.

Although the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) has increased the number of US children with coverage, insurance coverage alone does not guarantee access to needed health care. Angier et al. found affordability and lack of availability to be the most commonly reported barriers to health care access in a cohort of parents with incomes less than 133% of the federal poverty level; despite their child having health insurance, parents were unable to receive necessary health

care services.56 This is similar to reports from other studies highlighting lack of affordable and available care as major access barriers. Low socioeconomic status is associated with poor health status before, during, and after pregnancy.

The disturbing increases in racial and ethnic disparities in infant and neonatal mortality may be related to additional inequities in the provision of health care. Although the United States has always been a nation of immigrants, recent statelevel immigrant policies have made it much more difficult to address health inequities seen by race and ethnicity. Several states are seeking to criminalize immigrants, even those who are pregnant.57 A recent study analyzed birth record data from all 50 states and the District of Columbia in 2018, as well as state-level indicators of inclusive and criminalizing immigrant policies. More inclusive policies led to a reduction in preterm birth for those mothers born outside of the United States; in contrast, each additional criminalizing policy was associated with a 5% increase in preterm birth among Black women born outside the United States.57

Increased state-level Medicaid reimbursement for care increases adequate prenatal care utilization.

### Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

It is unlikely that improving care in the NICU alone will have a dramatic impact on reducing the US neonatal and infant mortality rates. However, by addressing and improving the significant health disparities and racial and ethnic differences seen in outcomes, there can be marked improvements in this indicator of US population health. It is important to investigate the areas of greatest impact that will result in improving maternal and neonatal health, as well as which local, state, and national initiatives can result in significant improvements in outcomes. First, all women, but especially those at highest risk such as non-Hispanic Black women and Native American/Alaska women and Pacific Islanders, must have improved health status even before conception. Programs that can screen and identify women at risk must be implemented. Maternal and child health care must be easily accessible, affordable, and equitable for all. This is certainly a challenge in very rural/ remote areas where health care access is limited or nonexistent and mortality rates are higher compared with urban areas.67

Access to adequate health care is also a challenge on most of the reservations and pueblos where many Native Americans reside. In addition, many urban settings have a maldistribution of health care providers and poor access to affordable transportation, making access difficult to those most in need.

The causes of poor maternal health, including obesity, diabetes, and hypertension, are multifactorial, but chronic maternal stress related to racial and ethnic disparities seen in the United States may also play a significant role. Screening and health promotion for obesity, diabetes, and hypertension are critical to improving the health of the mother. Current models of physician reimbursement discourage the significant time needed for such interventions. Innovative models, such as mobile clinics, group counseling, and specially trained health care workers have all shown to improve health outcomes in women of childbearing age. Chronic conditions, such as hypertension and diabetes must be well controlled over time, with continued and affordable access to medications that are known to be effective. The current dramatic increase in obesity, especially in the South and among non-Hispanic Blacks, Native Americans, and Hispanics in the United States, is a particular challenge. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) has recently published Clinical Management Guidelines for the management of obesity in pregnancy.68 This guideline offers an integrated approach to the management of obesity in women of reproductive age who are planning a pregnancy because of the concern for adverse outcomes. It also acknowledges the difficulty in successfully treating obesity in this population. Not often recognized is the lack of healthy food available in underserved and rural areas, as well as urban food deserts, which contributes to this problem. Similar to obesity management, mothers must be screened and treated for diabetes, hypertension, and renal disease before and during pregnancy. This will reduce many of the adverse outcomes seen in neonates and infants.

Other modifiable factors must be addressed for women at risk of becoming pregnant. Tobacco, alcohol, narcotics, and illicit substance use/abuse all have negative impacts on pregnancy outcomes and are often disproportionately used by those at highest risk of adverse outcomes. Culturally specific and appropriate educational materials and interventions must be available in a variety of settings, including schools. Tobacco cessation programs specifically during pregnancy, especially quitting early in pregnancy, have been shown to decrease the risk of preterm birth, especially if cessation occurs prior to conception.69 Alcohol use and abuse is particularly high among Native American and Alaska Natives and results in high rates of fetal alcohol syndrome.70 Fetal alcohol syndrome/fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is the largest cause of preventable long-term neurodevelopmental disability in children. Treatment of those ingesting alcohol during pregnancy is particularly difficult. However, intensive interventions have made some impact.71 Finally, the current opioid epidemic has been well publicized, as has the impact on those at the lowest socioeconomic populations. Pregnant women are often the least likely to get medical help given the highly punitive

However, programs that deal with multiple aspects of maternal drug use with known effective interventions and a less punitive approach have been shown to significantly improve neonatal and maternal outcomes, including more controlled or even cessation of drug use.72 Other innovative prenatal care programs such as group-based centering, easier access to care during pregnancy, and culturally centered care models also have been shown to have a significant impact on avoiding adverse outcomes of pregnancy.73

Renewed efforts must be made to improve the prepregnancy health of the mother. An important factor is access to health care and health insurance. Medicaid provides health insurance to those poorest Americans including the “working poor,” but this coverage is still woefully inadequate. Recent efforts have been made by the federal government to expand Medicaid coverage, but many states with significant minority populations, as well as eligible non-Hispanic Whites, have declined to expand eligibility for their Medicaid programs. Recent federal initiatives to provide even greater incentives to states have been only partially successful. Adults in Medicaid expansion states reported better coverage and access rates, narrower disparities between groups, and greater improvements across nearly every measure between 2013 and 2019.74 Interestingly, Hispanic adults continue to have the highest percentage of uninsured population, perhaps a reflection of concerns about immigration status/noncitizenship and subsequent adverse consequences of accessing the medical system. The most recent years since 2016 have seen a further deterioration in Medicaid coverage for all those in the United States, especially for Hispanics and non-Hispanic Blacks.

Access to insurance coverage before, during, and after pregnancy is also a vital piece of health care and improving maternal and infant outcomes. Having health insurance reduces racial and ethnic disparities in key measures of pregnancy for health care access and affordability, even after adjusting for income and other factors. Medicaid is currently the largest payor for maternity care in the United States. Implementation of the ACA and Medicaid expansion has decreased racial and ethnic disparities in insurance and access, and more quality-of-care measures are improving than worsening for racial and ethnic minority groups. However, many disparities have not changed, and overall progress is modest.75 Based on data from 2011 to 2016, state Medicaid expansion was not significantly associated with differences in rates of low birth weight or preterm birth outcomes overall, although there were significant improvements in relative disparities for non-Hispanic Black infants compared with for non-Hispanic White infants in states that expanded Medicaid versus those that did not.75 In contrast, a study by Bhatt did show that overall infant mortality rate decline was greater in Medicaid expansion states, with greater declines among non-Hispanic Black infants.76 Recent data indicate that insurance source can impact neonatal outcomes. A study by Kim et al. looked at infant mortality by payment source for delivery in the United States. They found overall infant mortality was lower in mothers who paid with private

insurance than in those who paid with Medicaid insurance (relative risk [RR] = 0.91 in 2017), but it was higher in self-paid women than in Medicaid-insured women at delivery (RR = 1.16, in 2017). Non-Hispanic Black (RR = 1.16 in 2017) and Hispanic (RR = 1.22 in 2017) mothers with self-payment had a higher risk for infant mortality than those with Medicaid at delivery. They found newborns whose mothers have no health insurance are more vulnerable to infant mortality than Medicaid beneficiaries, and non-Hispanic White ethnic groups with self-payment have an elevated risk of infant mortality among other racial and ethnic groups.77

As noted earlier, the ACA has significantly decreased the uninsured in the United States, with varying improvements based on states’ Medicaid expansion. This program has also mandated insurance coverage by all health plans for prenatal, postnatal, and infant care. Nonetheless, minority women and children in the United States are still less likely to be insured. The CHIP funded by the United States has increased coverage of uninsured children. Survey-based research shows positive associations between CHIP expansions and children’s health care utilization. Thus continued access to insurance for women and children is likely to have a significant impact on reducing the disparities seen in health outcomes in the United States. Unlike other developed countries, the United States has no universal health care, and the ACA has been a significant, albeit controversial, improvement in this area. Those in health care, both providers and insurers, must advocate for the most vulnerable in the population to maintain and expand this coverage.

Women often qualify for Medicaid coverage once the pregnancy is identified but cannot access the health care system before the pregnancy to improve their health, thus putting them at greater risk. Medicaid coverage increases during pregnancy for those mothers that are noninsured or underinsured. Recent federal efforts have also focused on increasing current postpartum coverage from 6 weeks to 12 months to improve the care of the mother while her child is young and for the next pregnancy. Data for new mothers with Medicaidcovered prenatal care in 2015 to 2018 from 43 states participating in the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) found that 26.8% of new mothers with Medicaid-covered prenatal care were uninsured before pregnancy, 21.9% became uninsured 2 to 6 months postpartum, and 34.5% were uninsured in either period, with higher perinatal uninsurance rates in nonexpansion states and for Hispanic women who completed the PRAMS survey in Spanish.78 Together, these findings indicate that, despite recent coverage gains, further policy change is needed to help women maintain health insurance coverage before and after pregnancy and to allow them to address ongoing health issues including obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and depression. Another public health initiative which will have a significant impact on health care disparities in the perinatal and neonatal period is in pregnancy delay, short interpregnancy intervals, and prevention of unintended pregnancies. Improved education about pregnancy prevention, including in the schools, as well as easier access to contraception, is critical. In addition, long-acting reproductive contraception (LARC) has been shown to be particularly effective and is reversible at the time of desired pregnancy. Contraception for those who desire it must be more readily available, especially immediately after delivery of a baby. Contraceptive counseling is rarely done during postpartum care or while a baby is in the NICU, but these are valuable missed opportunities to improve the health of the mother and her future children. Improved access to contraception will also increase interpregnancy intervals. Short interpregnancy intervals less than 6 months are more common in non-Hispanic Black mothers (7.1%) compared with non-Hispanic White mothers (4.1%) and Hispanic mothers (5.0%).82 The shortest interval of interpregnancy conception (<6 months) has been shown to have the highest adverse outcomes, especially in teen mothers.83 Access to contraception, especially for teen pregnancies, of which three-fourths are unintended, is critical to lengthen interpregnancy intervals and prevent adverse outcomes associated with teen pregnancy. Local legislation will be important to this public health intervention. For unwanted pregnancies, or for women that feel they cannot support having another child, abortion is an option. However, many states are considering or have implemented restrictions on abortion, especially those states with high minority populations. In addition, there are racial disparities in abortion rates for women of lower socioeconomic status and women of color. Hispanic women and non-Hispanic Black women have an up to fourfold higher rate of abortion than non-Hispanic White women.84 Recent efforts to decrease access to abortion for these women may only widen the health disparities for future generations.

As noted earlier, there are significant disparities in rates of prenatal care related to race and ethnicity, with non- Hispanic Blacks overall having the lowest rates of adequate

prenatal care and the highest rates of no prenatal care (see Table 8.1). Innovative models must be investigated and implemented. Statewide Medicaid-enhanced prenatal care programs have been shown to reduce infant mortality risk.85 Implementation of such a program in Michigan reduced the odds of infant death by 27%, with the highest reduction in Black infant mortality (29%). The greatest reduction was seen in those women who fully participated in the program using a population-based home visitation program to improve outcomes. For non-Hispanic Black women, this program further resulted in lower odds of low birth weight (0.76), very low birth weight (0.42), and very preterm birth (0.41) compared with matched nonparticipants.86

Although the underlying cause of prematurity is multifactorial and not clearly understood, certain interventions have been shown to reduce preterm birth. For those women identified with a singleton pregnancy and a previous history of spontaneous preterm birth, 17 alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17P) has been shown to reduce the risk of subsequent preterm delivery by up to 30%.87 However, access to this medication requires weekly injections, and the current drug delivery and reimbursement model is problematic for both physicians and women at risk. Many state Medicaid plans are investigating novel methods to deliver this drug to mothers at risk, given its known effectiveness.

Breastfeeding has been shown to have important benefits to both the mother and infant, including decreased breast and ovarian cancer rates and less postpartum depression and osteoporosis in the mother, as well as fewer infections, less risk of diabetes, heart disease, and asthma in the infant. Breastfeeding also has a significant impact on infant mortality. More importantly, breastfeeding initiation is significantly associated with reduced odds of post-perinatal infant death in multiple racial and ethnic groups within the US population.88 However, significant disparities exist in the rates of breastfeeding among different races and ethnicities.89 Non-Hispanic Black women have the lowest rates of initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding at 6 months, and any breastfeeding at 12 months. The disparities in adjusted breastfeeding rates have also become larger between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White infants in recent years. In addition, certain areas of the United States with the highest poverty levels, such as the Deep South and Appalachian states, have the lowest rates of breastfeeding. However, targeted interventions can be successful in improving breastfeeding rates in this part of the United States. After implementing the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding program in delivery hospitals in four Southern states, the disparity in breastfeeding initiation between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White infants decreased by 9.6% over the course of 31 months.90 Breastfeeding initiation increased from 66% to 75% for all races combined, and exclusivity increased from 34% to 39%. Initiation and exclusive breastfeeding among non-Hispanic Black infants increased from 46% to 63% and from 19% to 31%, respectively. Successful implementation of breastfeeding must begin before delivery with targeted and appropriate education. Baby-friendly initiatives in the United States have resulted in increased awareness of the importance of this public health
